claims.claim: Aramini calls Wolfe the ultimate engineer, disputing any reading of him as a deconstructive author.
claims.page: answer to John Grayshaw on critical interest

claims.claim: Aramini says Wolfe frequently changed his style and worked across multiple genres.
claims.quote: Wolfe frequently changed his style and worked in multiple genres

claims.claim: Aramini says the erudite banter of Jack Vance's rogues informed vocabulary choices in The Book of the New Sun.
Aramini reports Wolfe learned Greek for the Latro books and read original sources.
claims.quote: He learned Greek for the Latro books, read original sources

claims.claim: Aramini says the way allegory is embedded in Wolfe changes from story to story.
claims.quote: the way that allegory is embedded changes from story to

claims.claim: Gordon calls the style of The Fifth Head of Cerberus, Peace and The Book of the New Sun elegant and baroque, and says she wants Wolfe to return to it.
claims.quote: the elegant and baroque style of The Fifth Head

claims.claim: Wolfe's narrator, quoted by Gordon, states in a plain aphorism that cultures die like people.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, A Borrowed Man (2015), quoted in Joan Gordon, LARB, 3 March 2016
claims.quote: Cultures are like people, it seems

claims.claim: Gordon identifies one embedded passage of the narrator's older writing inside the plain late novel as evoking the New Sun style.
claims.quote: a passage that evokes the style of The Book

claims.claim: Gaiman says Wolfe keeps trying new ways of writing.
claims.source: Neil Gaiman, 'My hero: Gene Wolfe', The Guardian, 13 May 2011
claims.quote: he keeps trying new ways of writing

claims.claim: Robinson says Wolfe shifts his pacing very freely throughout his stories.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: Wolfe shifts his pacing everywhere in his stories very freely

claims.claim: Robinson says there is no telling whether a Wolfe sentence will cover a second or a year.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: if it will cover a second or a year

claims.claim: Robinson faults volumes written entirely at one pace, whether plodding or frenetic, as predictable.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: written entirely at the same pace, either plodding or frenetic

claims.claim: Robinson likens reading Wolfe after uniformly paced fiction to hearing music after a metronome.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: as on music after a metronome

claims.feature: other: analytic syntax on pulp matter
claims.claim: Robinson characterises the mature Wolfe voice as Proust-like syntax, precision and analytical power applied to pulp material.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: syntax, sensibility, precision, and analytical power reminiscent of Proust

claims.claim: Robinson argues Wolfe's stories are usually not allegories but events in themselves.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: not allegories but events in themselves
